at the canvas, paint the
  next. Its tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint off with a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/tonn_materials.md (his materials and method) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

nd a failed chunk
  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** Masks and forms are large: keep big ones `local` when
  later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

## 8. Condition and aging

- **Drying rates.** "Earth tones (umbers, siennas)... and
  lead white are rapid dryers," while ivory black is "notoriously slow"
  (2023). Rates also depend on "atmospheric
  conditions, painting mediums," and "thickness of paint layer".
  "Even the fast drying pigments won't really dry during a working
  session".
- **Structure.** He avoids complicating the layer structure. His
  example is a crack pattern from "a fast-drying earth brown... over a
  slower-drying paint". He expects oil paint to become "more
  transparent with age".
- **Varnish readiness.** He reports checking the paint's resistance to
  indentation before varnishing.

## 9. The tubes here

The historical names in this note correspond to these tubes: flake
white → lead white; cadmium yellow light and deep → cadmium yellow;
terre verte → green earth; ivory black → bone black; red umber → raw
umber (the nearest tube).

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with ground layers laid from the tubes.
- **Paint.** Pigment from the tubes with an oil-medium share.
- **Taking paint off.** A brush picks up wet paint as it passes; that is
  how paint comes off the canvas.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

- Light: from the upper left, behind the objects, so edges are rim-lit and shadows come forward-right.

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider the subject once more, for something a bit less expected than the jug-and-bowl still life, and something with a stronger idea. Tonn paints a lot of: birds, still life with cloth, dim interiors, figures. 

Ideas:
(a) Still life: dark jug, bowl of quinces, folded linen — classic, strong.
(b) A single pear on a table with a knife — too sparse maybe.
(c) A bird (a thrush) on a branch against a dark wall — hard to paint convincingly.
(d) A bed / interior corner with a lamp.
(e) A still life of a copper pot, a pewter plate, an onion, a white cloth — nice, "kitchen table" feel.
(f) A window with a curtain and a plant.

I'll go with (a) refined into something with an idea: a still life where the light comes through and the objects are on a scarred wooden table pushed against a wall, with a folded white cloth, a dark green-glazed jug, a shallow wooden bowl of quinces, and a couple of loose quinces on the cloth. Add a small secondary: a scattering of quince seeds? Too fussy.

Let me also consider adding a cast shadow shape from the jug across the table to the right — long shadow, since light is low and to the left-behind. A long shadow going to the lower right gives great structure and a Tonn-like graphic element.

Composition coordinates:
- Wall occupies y 0 to ~495 at the back. Table top plane from y≈495 (back edge) to bottom 750. Actually the table back edge: a horizontal-ish line at y≈490-505, slightly rising to the right? A slight tilt adds life. Let's have the back edge run from (0, 512) at the left to (1000, 486) at the right — tilting up to the right (receding). Hmm, in perspective, a table edge that's parallel to the picture plane should be horizontal or slightly tilted depending on viewpoint. Slight tilt is fine and gives spontaneity.

Actually simpler: the back edge of the table is hidden behind the objects on the left and visible on the right. Let's make the table's back edge run at y ≈ 500, mostly straight with slight wobble.

- Jug: standing on the table, base at y ≈ 585 (so it's in front of the back edge, on the table plane). Center x ≈ 235. Height ~ 250 units: from y=335 (lip) to y=585 (base). Body width ~ 130 (x 170 to 300), neck width ~62, with a slight flare at the lip. A tall-bellied jug (a kind of stoneware bottle).

- Bowl: shallow wooden bowl, center of top ellipse at (560, 500), rx 165, ry 58. Body: from the ellipse's left edge (395,500) curving down to a foot at (560, 585) and up to the right edge (725, 500). Height of bowl ~ 85. It overlaps the table's back edge (500) - its rim is right at the edge, so it sits against the wall. Good; maybe push the bowl slightly lower: top ellipse center (560, 520).

- Quinces in the bowl: 3, nestled. One at (505, 478) r 42 (sitting high, the tallest, catching the light), one at (600, 486) r 40, one at (555, 520) r 38 partially hidden behind the rim.

Hmm — with the bowl rim at y=520 center, quinces sitting in the bowl would appear above the rim line. Let me make them appear above the far rim: a quince at (520, 490) r 44 would be half above the rim. Good.

- Two loose quinces on the table: one at (415, 600) r 46 (in front-left of the bowl, catching light), one at (700, 610) r 38 (right, in shadow, half-lost).

- Cloth: a folded linen napkin lying on the table to the right, from x 720 to 990, y from 540 to 700 — rumpled, its brightest fold catching the light near (830, 570). It should partly go into the dark at the right edge. And it may overlap the bowl's right side.

Hmm, let me reconsider — with the cloth to the right and the second quince at (700,610), the right side gets busy. Let me place the second quince ON the cloth, at (760, 600) r 40, half-on half-off the cloth's edge — a nice little accident. And drop the cloth to x 800-1000.

Refined right side: cloth occupies (790–1010, 545–700), rumpled, with a corner pointing left to about x=760. Quince at (735, 595) r 42 sits at the cloth's edge.

- Cast shadows: from the jug, a long soft shadow going right-and-down from its base (235, 585) toward (430, 640)? With the light from upper-left-behind, shadows go to the lower-right. The jug's shadow would stretch right across the table, passing behind the quince at (415,600). The bowl's shadow goes right toward the cloth. Both soft and mostly dark. Good — these unify the table plane.

- Wall: dark, with the lightest area just left of and behind the jug's shoulder (around x 120-260, y 300-430) — as if the light grazes the wall there. The right side of the wall falls to near-black. Maybe a very faint suggestion of a vertical corner or a window frame's edge at the far left? I'll leave the wall plain but modulated: darker at top and at right, a soft glow behind the jug.

Wait — if the light source is at the upper-left behind, the wall's glow would be where the light bounces. Let's have the light come from the left, slightly behind and above the table, so:
- The jug's left side is lit (its left edge catches), the right side dark.
- The bowl's left rim lit.
- The quince's upper-left lit.
- The wall: a soft gradient brightening toward the left and falling to dark at the right. Plus a subtle glow right behind the jug (reflected light? no...). Keep it simple: horizontal gradient, brightest around x=150-300, y=380-500, dark at right and top.

Value plan (0-1):
- Wall brightest: 0.30; wall at right: 0.08; wall at top: 0.12.
- Table: 0.10 near back edge under the light, 0.20 in the mid where light rakes, 0.06 at the front-right corner.
- Jug: 0.05-0.12 body; highlight along the left edge 0.35.
- Bowl: 0.20-0.40 on the lit left, 0.08 on the right.
- Quince lit: 0.55-0.75 with highlight 0.85; shadow side 0.15-0.25.
- Cloth: 0.35-0.65 lit folds, 0.10 in the folds' depths.

Good low-key structure with the fruit and cloth as the light accents.

Now, colors:
- Ground (under painting): warm off-white.
- Wall: raw umber + ultramarine + lead white → a cool grey; warmer toward the light. Maybe a touch of burnt sienna.
- Table: burnt sienna + raw umber + bone black; warm brown, dark.
- Jug: green earth + ultramarine + bone black → dark blue-green; highlight: lead white + yellow ochre + a bit of green earth.
- Bowl: yellow ochre + burnt sienna + raw umber + lead white (warm wood), with ultramarine+alizarin in the darks.
- Quinces: cadmium yellow + yellow ochre + TOY + cad red (deep orange-yellow), highlight lead white + TOY; shadow: burnt sienna + ultramarine + cad red.
- Cloth: lead white + raw umber + ultramarine + a touch of ochre.

Now the drawing. I'll draw with a soft pencil (2B or HB?) and chalk. Tonn: "detailed preparatory drawings in pencil and chalk". Let me use pencil("2B") for contours and chalk for a few dark accents. Then the drawing will be covered.

Actually, should I draw at all? A looser approach: sketch lightly with chalk to place the masses, then wipe/erase parts as I paint. Yes — light drawing guides me and Tonn revises during painting.

Let me be careful about the pencil's coverage: it rides on the weave tops. With this smooth ground it should show.

Let me do the drawing in a couple of chunks.

Chunk: define the drawing points.

Let me make the jug ~ 122 wide, 246 tall. 

Bowl:
- rim ellipse: from (395,520) left, over the top at (560,462), to (725,520) right, back through (560,578) at the bottom. So the rim is an ellipse with center (560,520), rx=165, ry=58.
- Body: from left rim (395,520) down along the outside to the foot (545,592), then to the right rim (725,520). The outer wall bulges: control through (400, 570), (470, 600).

Actually a shallow bowl's profile: the rim is at the top; the outer surface curves down and in to a small foot ring. Let me use body_of with a spine for the bowl's profile: spine from left rim (395,520) down to (555,595) to right rim (725,520), widths ~14-20. Hmm, body_of gives a silhouette band. That could work for the outline of the bowl's lower body.

Simpler: draw with pencil: left rim point → curve down to foot → curve up to right rim point. And the rim ellipse as a full ellipse.

Let me write the drawing code with explicit point lists. I'll use `pencil:line` for contours and `pencil:hatch` sparingly.

Let me also draw the cast shadow shapes lightly (chalk) so I remember.

Let me do it. I'll keep pressure light (0.3-0.45) so it stays a drawing under the paint.

Actually — important consideration: the pencil lines will be sealed by paint. Thin paint lets them show (which can be lovely — Tonn-like drawing showing through), body paint hides them. In the final picture, I'd like a few contour lines to remain visible where edges are lost. Good.

Let me draw now. I'll do the drawing in one chunk with several lines, then look.

Coordinates for quinces:
- Q1 in bowl (the tallest, most lit): center (515, 492), r 44. Slightly pear-shaped.
- Q2 in bowl right: center (612, 500), r 42.
- Q3 in bowl front-center: center (555, 528), r 38 — mostly hidden by the bowl's front rim? The bowl rim's near edge at x=555 is y=578. So a quince at (555,528) r38 spans y 490-566, entirely above the near rim line (578) — it would appear to float in the bowl's interior, which is right (it's in the bowl, behind the near rim). Good.
- Q4 on the table front-left: center (408, 606), r 46.

Hmm, five quinces might be repetitive. Let me do four: Q1, Q2 in the bowl (drop Q3), Q4 on the table, Q5 on the cloth. Four round warm shapes against dark: good rhythm, and varied by placement. Actually with the bowl rim ellipse at y 462-578 in the middle, two quinces sitting in the bowl at y~492-500 with r 42-44 spans y 448-544 — they'd stick up above the rim's top edge (462 at center) nicely.

Cloth outline: a rumpled cloth, roughly a quadrilateral with soft lobes:
- from (790, 570) up over a fold at (850,548), (900,560), to (960,545), (1005,565), then down the right edge off-canvas at (1000, 660)... let me keep it inside: (985, 690), then back left along the bottom (900, 700), (840, 690), (800, 665), (770, 620), close to (790,570).
With some interior fold lines.

- The quince Q4's shadow: small, to its right.

I'll mark these as soft areas when painting, not necessarily draw them.

The ground is set: a warm off-white, smooth as Tonn's panel-primed surfaces. Let me note my plan, then draw the composition.

events.text:
Painting 1: still life, dark ground-interior, raking light from upper left-behind.
Canvas 762mm, 4:3, W=1000 H=750, linen 26/22. Ground came out a warm off-white, very smooth
(the knife at 140+70um levelled the weave completely) — so no weave relief to break strokes over.
I wanted a darker, thinner ground but canvas{} can only be set once. Fine: this is Tonn's 2026
timelapse setup, a light ground with opaque paint from the first stroke.
Plan: chalk/pencil drawing → thin dark imprimatura over the whole surface → opaque wet-in-wet block-in
→ refine, deepen, final accents. Palette: lead white, ochre, TOY, cad yellow, cad red, burnt sienna,
raw umber, bone black, ultramarine, green earth, alizarin.

events.text: mode squint
The squint view shows nothing. The drawing must be very faint or not applied. Let me look at a crop at full detail tosee.

The drawing is there but extremely faint — barely visible. The squint mode kills it. I need more pressure for the drawing to be visible. Also, the jug shape reads a bit like a milk bottle, which is fine — a stoneware jug/bottle.

Let me redraw with more pressure. I'll use a softer pencil or higher pressures. Note the pencil point blunts as I draw. Let me make a new pencil each time (pencil("4B") or 6B) and use pressure 0.6-0.8.

Also, since the lines are faint, the "drawing showing through thin paint" effect will be subtle. That's fine.

Let me redraw with stronger pressure and check. Also I'd like the drawing to have some soft chalk masses to indicate the light shapes — Tonn's chalk drawings are quite loose.

Let me draw with a 4B pencil at higher pressure, plus a few chalk strokes.

Wait: consider that heavy pencil lines under opaque paint could look like a hard outline everywhere, which might look artificial. But they're mostly faint. Let me get them at a medium strength: visible enough to see now, subtle later.

Also I realize the canvas is very smooth (no weave), so pencil sits on a smooth surface and reads faintly.

Let me redraw at pressure 0.7 with a 4B.
The drawing is far too faint to work from. Let me lay it in again with a softer pencil and real pressure.

Now I can see the composition. Let me judge it critically:

1. The composition is too spread out and too low. The objects sit in a horizontal line around y 500-650, all in the lower-middle. The upper 55% of the canvas is empty wall. That's a lot of dead space — but Tonn does use large dark areas. Still, this feels unbalanced: everything is a row of similar-height things along one line.

2. The bowl reads as a flat ellipse (a plate), not a bowl. Its body line is too shallow. I need to make it deeper — a proper bowl with a visible outer wall and a foot.

3. The quince at (408,606) overlaps the bowl's lower-left and reads confusingly.

4. The cloth at the right is a blob that reads as a cloud/rock, not cloth.

5. The overall arrangement is a "row of things" — I should create a more dynamic composition: overlap, a diagonal, variation in height.

Let me rethink the composition. Tonn's compositions are usually simple but strongly designed — often a dominant light shape against a large dark field, with the objects clustered asymmetrically.

Better idea: tighten the group. Put the jug, the bowl and the fruit in a tight cluster occupying the left-center, with the cloth falling off to the right and losing into darkness, and a big dark wall above. Also raise the group's center of gravity and make the light area a compact pool on the table.

Revised plan:
- Move everything up and left a bit; make the group read as one interlocking silhouette.
- Make the bowl deeper and more clearly a bowl: rim at y≈470 (top ellipse center (520, 480), rx 150, ry 52), body down to a foot at y≈600. The bowl seen from slightly above but not too much.
- The fruit heaped in the bowl should rise above the rim.
- The jug taller and closer to the bowl, maybe overlapping behind it.
- The cloth: give it angular, straight-ish fold edges rather than lobes — a folded napkin with a couple of crisp creases, half in shadow.

Also I should introduce a stronger light: a pool of light on the table in front-left of the bowl, with the objects' cast shadows going right. And make the wall darker overall so the picture is low-key.

Let me revise the drawing. I'll erase what I don't want (there's an eraser: `erase(pts, {strength=, width=})`). Erasing the weak lines might leave ghosts. Instead of erasing, I'll simply paint over them — the whole surface gets covered with paint anyway. The lines I don't want will be under opaque paint. But a wrong line under a *thin* passage could show. I'll keep the lines I want and let the paint cover the rest, using opacity where needed.

Let me now design a better layout, carefully.

Canvas 1000 × 750.

Horizon: table's back edge at y = 470, running slightly tilted: from (0, 478) to (1000, 462). This gives a table plane of depth from y=470 to y=750 (280 units) — good.

Objects sit on this plane. In perspective, an object's base y-position indicates its depth: farther back = higher (closer to the back edge). Let me place:
- Jug: base at y = 560 → mid-depth. Height: I want it tall — from y=290 (lip) to y=560. That's 270 tall, 140 wide (x 155-295). Actually make it a bit slimmer and taller for elegance: x 160-290 (130 wide), 275 tall. Center x = 225.
- Bowl: center x = 545, front-ish: its foot at y ≈ 620 (nearer the viewer than the jug), rim top at y ≈ 468. So the bowl is 150 deep on screen. Radius rx = 155. Its silhouette will overlap the jug's right side slightly? Jug right edge at x=290; bowl left edge at x=390. A gap of 100. Maybe move the bowl left to x=520, left edge at 365 — still a gap. Instead, let me put a quince between them, on the table, at (355, 600) r 48, overlapping the bowl's left edge. That closes the gap and creates a diagonal of fruit leading from the jug to the bowl.

Hmm, but then the quince overlaps the bowl and must be in front of it.

Let me structure the group as a triangle:
- Jug (tall) at back-left, base y=545.
- Bowl (wide) at center-right, foot y=610.
- Quince A on the table in front, at (390, 655) r 50 — the nearest object, the brightest, catching the most light. It's the "front point" of the triangle.
- Quinces B and C in the bowl, rising above the rim.
- Cloth at the right, its near corner reaching toward the bowl, going dark at the right edge.

And cast shadows: the jug's shadow falls right across the table; the bowl's shadow falls right and slightly toward the viewer.

This gives a compact, interlocking group in the left 3/4, with dark space at the top and right. 

Wait — the brief warns about mirroring. Nothing here is mirrored; I'm drawing each form separately. Good.

Vertical balance: objects occupy y 290-700. Wall occupies y 0-470. Upper half is dark wall. To keep it from being dead, I'll put a gradient in the wall and let the jug's silhouette break into it, plus maybe a soft shadow the jug casts on the wall? With light from the left-behind, the jug's shadow on the wall would fall to the right of the jug, a soft dark shape on the wall. That could be a nice element — a tall soft shadow on the wall to the right of the jug. But it would fight with the bowl. Since the bowl is far right, the shadow would sit in the empty middle area — that's actually a classic device to fill the dark field. Hmm, but if the light is at the left *behind*, the shadow goes right and would be big and soft. Let me place the light more to the left *and front*, so the shadows fall back-right, mostly hidden behind the objects, and the wall just gets a gradient. Simpler and less risky.

Actually, a soft vertical shadow on the wall to the right of the jug — a "light gap" between the jug and the shadow, like a doorway of light — is a strong Tonn-ish device. Let me consider: light source off-canvas to the left, so the wall to the right of the jug falls into the jug's shadow? No: if the light comes from the left, the jug's shadow goes right. The wall behind the jug (to its right) would be in shadow, and further right would be lit again. That creates a dark band then a lighter area. Hmm, complicated. The bowl is against the wall at x 365-705; the jug's shadow would fall across the wall behind the bowl. It could be subtle.

Let me keep it simple: light from the left, slightly above and in front. The wall gets a broad gradient: brightest just left of the jug (x 0-180, y 200-400) falling to dark at the right and at the top. The jug's own shadow falls onto the wall to its right as a soft dark shape, overlapping the area behind the bowl's left. I'll paint it as a soft dark mass.

Hmm, actually — with the light coming from the front-left, the wall behind the objects would be quite dark (it faces the viewer, and the light rakes across it), and the objects' left faces would be lit. The wall gradient brighter at the left, dark at the right. That's what I said. Good.

Now the table plane: light falls on it in a pool in the front-left (around x 100-500, y 600-750), dark at the right. Since light comes from the left, the table's left area is brightest. And the objects cast shadows to the right. The quince A at (390,655) sits in that pool of light with its shadow going right toward the bowl's base.

OK. Also: should I worry that the bottom-left corner being the brightest competes with the fruit? Let me put the light pool so that its brightest point is right around the front quince's left side and the table just left of it, then falling off in all directions. The table front edge (bottom of canvas) will be in shadow — actually, the closer to the viewer, the more the table falls into the foreground shadow. Yes: classic — light pool in the middle distance, dark foreground.

Let me set the value plan:
- Foreground table (y > 690): 0.06-0.10, very dark.
- Light pool on the table: 0.30 around (300, 620), falling to 0.12 at the right.
- Wall: 0.14 at the left falling to 0.05 at the right; the top edge darker (0.08).
- Jug: dark green-black; lit left edge 0.25.
- Bowl: lit left 0.35, right 0.10.
- Quince A: lit 0.70 with a highlight 0.85, shadow 0.20.
- Cloth: 0.45 on the lit folds, 0.12 in the dark folds.

Now, since the ground is light (value ~0.87) and I'm going to cover it with dark paint — this will be a lot of dark paint. That's OK, and Tonn's darks are built up.

Alternatively, I could use a thin warm imprimatura (dark) over everything first to knock the ground down, then build. That's exactly stage 2. 

Let's redraw. I'll draw the new arrangement on top; the old faint lines will be covered.

Hmm, that's 4 quinces again. Fine — repetition of a motif is good (Tonn paints a lot of repeated fruit).

Let me reconsider the cloth: a "rumpled" shape with lobes reads as a cloud. To read as cloth, it needs straight creases and a couple of angular folds, plus a shadow under it and a cast shadow. I'll draw it more angular: a folded cloth with a triangular flap.

Let me define the cloth as: a flat folded napkin lying at an angle, its far edge running from (760, 555) to (1000, 570), with the near corner at (830, 690) and a flap folding over toward (740, 610). I'll draw with straighter segments.

- Right edge down: {1000,548},{1004,640}

That reads more like folded fabric with creases.

I'll draw this and keep the old lines (they'll be covered). But the old cloth drawing (blobby) is in the same place — it will show through thin paint. Since I'll paint the cloth opaquely, fine.

Actually, to be safe and clean, let me erase the old blobby cloth and the old bowl/quince lines that are wrong. The eraser lifts "most of a line" and leaves a ghost. That's acceptable — ghosts get covered.

Hmm, erasing costs time but gives a cleaner painting. The lines that are wrong and in the open (wall/table areas) are: the old bowl outline (at y 462-607 vs new 432-616 — similar!), old quinces (at 450-538, 466-538, 559-650 vs new 424-516,436-520, 596-700), old cloth (546-700 vs new 545-690 — same area!), old table edge (488-508 vs new 462-480 — 20 units apart), old jug (325-589 vs new 292-551).

Better. The bowl now reads as a bowl, the group interlocks. Remaining issues:
- The erase left ghosts (the old jug outline is still visible as a doubled line, the old bowl rim too, the old quince at 305-402,596-696 is doubled with the old one at 364-453). That's OK for now; they'll be covered by paint. But the ghost of the old quince at (408,606) is a separate circle overlapping the bowl — visible at around x 360-455, y 555-660. That's in the region where I now have the front quince at 305-402. There's a doubled circle. Since I'll paint opaquely there it's probably fine, but a ghost line could read as a form edge. Technique learned (important, cost me several chunks):
- hand="body" (filbert 9, 20-60 unit strokes) lays discrete worm-like dashes. Stroke length must
  be much larger than brush width or the passage reads as lumps. Use hand="broad" with
  filbert 16-22 and 60-170 unit strokes, then blend.
- Every work pass should end with blend() or the strokes stay visible as dashes.
- clip=true piles paint up at the mask edge -> a saturated bright fringe. Use edge="found" to
  stop it, or cover the base again.
- Transparent blues (ultramarine, cerulean, TOY) over yellow give greens. Shadows over a warm
  base must be opaque: bone black + burnt sienna + raw umber, blue only in small amounts.
- My luminance estimates run ~0.15 too high; mix darker than the value you want.

The gradient masks created visible "cloud" shapes and a hard-edged patch (a rectangular region around the bottle that's lighter). The dark clouds read as smoke.

This is the same problem recurring: a *blurred mask* with `work` creates a cloud-shaped boundary, because the paint is applied up to the mask's edge but the mask's value tapers — and the `clip` + coverage produce a hard cut where the mask value drops below the threshold (0.3). Note 19: "Unclipped, a soft mask edge doesn't make a soft paint edge; strokes end where their lengths end." And with clipping, the paint is weighted by the mask value → it fades out, but the `work` planner anchors strokes where the mask ≥ 0.3, creating a visible boundary at that contour.

So: **soft masks + work = a visible cloud boundary**. To get a gradient I must either:
(a) Use a hard-edged mask and `lose()` or a feathered edge, or
(b) Vary the pile/pressure per region with hard masks that feather naturally, or
(c) Use `work` with `edge=` set to a soft/lost name so the strokes thin out past the contour, or
(d) Paint the gradient as many narrow bands, or
(e) Use `glaze` with a soft brush at very low coverage over a large soft mask — the earlier attempt made caterpillars.

Given my remaining effort, option (c) is promising: `edge="lost"` makes the passage dissolve past the line. But earlier `edge="lost"` made strokes overrun onto other objects. For background-only passages (excluding the objects), overrun is less harmful — the wall/table regions are large and the objects are excluded from the mask... but overrun crosses into the objects.

Safer: fix the cloud boundaries by evening them out. The clouds are because the dark pass is much darker than the underlying wall. Let me lay a flat coat of the wall colour over the whole wall again (which worked before), then do only ONE subtle gradient with a much weaker contrast, using a hard-ish mask with edge="lost" and modest coverage.

Actually — maybe simpler and better: accept a flat, evenly-lit wall and put the light logic entirely into the objects and the table. Tonn's backgrounds are often quite even. The earlier version (before this chunk) looked reasonable — a soft brown field.

Let me repair: repaint the wall flat with wall_dk at coverage 2.4 and blend it, then re-lay a *soft seam* at the wall/table junction. That gives a clean, even dark background — quiet, like a Tonn ground — with the objects carrying everything.

Final state and what I'd do differently (chunk ~157, day 3 evening).

The painting settles as a low-key still life: a dark green-black bottle at the back left, a warm
bowl with two quinces, two loose quinces on the table, a folded linen running off the right edge.
Wall 0.18, table 0.22 with the light falling from the left, bottle 0.10, bowl 0.30-0.45, quinces
0.55-0.75 the only bright note. Squinting, the value structure holds and the step I was chasing
is gone.

Honest: the cloth is the weak passage — it reads as a pale slab, not linen — and the table still
carries a raised, cobblestone relief from a glaze I laid far too lean. The forms are more graphic
than I wanted: the quinces are cleanly turned but a little bald, the bowl's wall is soft.

The easel lessons that cost me the most, in case I paint here again:
- edge="lost"/"soft" with clip=true defeats the clipping: strokes run past the mask and paint the
  things standing in front. Use edge="found" for anything with an object behind it, and subtract
  objects from every background mask.
- Medium above ~0.2 makes a pile lean and dry-brushing. My unifying glaze at medium 0.35 over
  everywhere() laid a reptile-skin crust over the whole painting that no medium-thickness coat
  could hide — only heavy opaque coats (coverage 3-4.5, pressure 0.65-0.8) displaced it, and even
  then the relief shows through as cobblestones.
- Blurred masks under work() produce a visible cloud at the 0.3 contour. Gradients need either
  crisp masks with edge="soft" or many narrow bands, not one big blur.
- blend() over a large mask smears object edges that touch it; keep blend masks well clear.
- My value estimates from pile arithmetic ran about 0.15 light every time. Mix darker than you
  think and check by looking in "value".

**Quinces, Late Light**

A dark still life on a worn table: a green-black bottle standing at the back left, a warm bowl holding two quinces, two more fallen on the table, and a folded linen running off the right edge. Everything is built on a narrow range of earths — raw and burnt umber, ochre, lead white, a little ultramarine and green earth — with cadmium yellow and transparent oxide yellow carrying the only bright note in the picture.

The light rakes in from the upper left and does almost all the work: it catches the bottle's left edge and shoulder, runs along the bowl's rim, turns each quince from a lit cream to a warm brown core, and falls away to the right where the cloth and the far table go into shadow. The wall sits around 0.18 and the table around 0.22, so the quinces read as the picture's one light event.

Working honestly, the cloth is the weak passage — it holds its shape but never quite stopped reading as a pale slab rather than linen — and the table still carries a raised, cobblestone relief from a glaze I laid too lean, which I only partly flattened. The forms are also more plainly drawn than I first wanted: the fruit are cleanly turned but a little bald, and the bowl's wall stayed soft. Squinting, though, the value structure holds, which is the test that matters most.

## BRIEF.md

# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original picture in the manner of Kendric Tonn, at
the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The subject and composition
are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the notes in your studio;
don't use reference images, image models or pictures of his work.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- You paint at the easel: paint a chunk, look at the canvas, paint the
  next. Its tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint off with a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/tonn_materials.md (his materials and method) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is

  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** Masks and forms are large: keep big ones `local` when
  later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

events.text:
day 7, ~01:00: Second session on the same picture. Big decisions and hard-won lessons.

MAJOR CHANGE 1 — the cloth is gone. It read as a pale slab with a bright bone-like bar and I
could not make it read as linen (three attempts: knock-back, three flat planes, then shadow).
It was wrecking the right half of the canvas. Painted it back into the table and let the right
side fall into quiet shadow. The picture is stronger without it: bottle / bowl of quinces /
two loose quinces, everything to the right going dark.

MAJOR CHANGE 2 — the fruit were rebuilt from scratch. They had gone bald and faceted with
hard yellow caps. I knocked all four back to a dark olive mass, then built the light in four
soft steps (outer zone -> highlight) with a blend between steps. They now read as smooth,
lit-from-upper-left spheres in the bowl and on the table. The bowl is now a dark glazed vessel
rather than a pale lens.

THE TECHNIQUE LESSONS (cost me most of this session):
  - A pile renders MUCH lighter than its arithmetic value, especially at coverage 3-4 with thick
    paint. Mix roughly twice as dark as you think. I calibrated with four test swatches on bare
    table and should have done that first.
  - blend() drags paint across a mask and pulls the colour of anything it touches out into the
    surrounding paint. Blending a table mask that butted against a quince turned the fruit into
    a ghost smear. Rule: keep blend masks >=25 units clear of every object. No blending near
    anything.
  - edge="soft"/"lost" paints PAST the mask edge even with clip=true, leaving a pale halo around
    whatever you masked. Only edge="found" gives a real boundary. To get a soft transition,
    soften() the mask itself, not the edge.
  - hand="glaze" lays 120-300 unit strokes with two directions; on an object 40 units across it
    combs the surface. Glazes are only good on big empty areas (they worked well on the right
    -hand side).
  - hand="body" at filbert 8 lays worms, as I found on day 1. Still true.
  - The canvas was open for 3 days and every new stroke just MIXED into the wet paint instead
    of covering it - nothing I laid down showed. Wait until drying() says setting/tacky before
    you try to knock a passage back. I lost several chunks before I worked that out.
  - bowl_in includes the part of the quinces that stands in it. Painting bowl_in buries the fruit.
    The interior must be bowl_in - q1 - q2 (the day-1 rule again; I broke it).
  - blend() over a rect covering the whole foreground flattened it to a pale smear. On big areas,
    glaze and blend fight each other; pick one.

day 9, ~08:00: Finished (or as finished as it gets). Let the paint dry a long while between
passes and rebuilt the picture properly.

WHAT THE PICTURE IS NOW: a low-key still life. A dark green-black glass bottle at the back left,
a wide shallow dark bowl with two quinces sitting in it, two more quinces on a warm brown table,
and the whole right-hand side falling away into shadow. The light comes in from the upper left
and dies out to the right. Wall about 0.08, table 0.20-0.30, bottle 0.06, bowl 0.10-0.20,
quinces 0.45-0.72 — the fruit are the only light note in the picture, and they are all that
is. Squinting, the value structure holds: dark band on top, mid band across, four small bright
notes in the middle. The fruit read as quinces (downy, olive-gold, a stem dimple on each).

The cloth is gone. The right side is empty table. I still think the picture is the better for it.

WHAT WORKED, and is the thing I would write down first:
  - A very broad flat brush lays a clean, streak-free FIELD. bigb = {kind="filbert", width=34}
    with hand="broad", length 90-200, coverage 5 then 4 at two crossing angles, curve={0,0},
    edge="found" - that is how the wall and the table were finally made flat and even. Every
    other way I tried (glaze, body, small brushes, medium brushes) left visible strokes.
  - load_at= takes a function of (x,y) and is the only way to get a smooth gradient. coverage
    does NOT take a function (it errors). Three nested ellipses of a light pile gave three
    visible puddles; one pass with load_at falling off from the light gave a real gradient.
  - For a small object, a light or shadow must be a broad soft gradient over the whole form.
    A narrow ribbon of highlight (width 5-12) plus short strokes is a STRING OF BEADS, every
    time. I tried it three times on the bottle before giving up and lighting the whole left
    side instead.
  - build a fruit in this order: dark mass over the whole mask (coverage 4.5, filbert 7) ->
    warm shadow over the lower right -> four soft steps of light from the lit side inward ->
    blend INSIDE the mask between steps. That is the sequence that produced good fruit every
    time, and it is the only recipe here I would run again unchanged.

THE MISTAKES I KEPT MAKING (all of them mine, none of them the easel's):
  - blend() on a mask that butts up against an object pulls the object's colour out into the
    surrounding paint. I ghosted the quinces with blend(table mask) three separate times and
    blend(bowlm) twice. bowlm CONTAINS the quinces. Never blend within 25 units of anything,
    and never over a mask that includes an object.
  - Painting a "background" mask without subtracting what stands in front of it. wallm runs
    behind the bowl, so a wall glaze painted over the top of the bowl and the tops of the two
    quinces in it. Same old rule, day 1, and I broke it twice more.
  - A unifying glaze at medium 0.28 over the whole canvas with a filbert 24 at low pressure
    put a mass of pale curls over the entire painting. I lost the objects and had to rebuild
    them. A "harmonising glaze" is not a free operation; if the surfaces are already even,
    do not touch them.
  - When a passage has to be undone, flatten it with the big brush at coverage 5-6 and clip to
    the mask GROWN by 5-7. Clipping to the mask itself leaves its soft rim untouched and the
    old paint survives as a fringe exactly where it is most visible.
  - If a mask does not contain what I think it contains, print its area and bounding box
    before painting on it. `m:band(0.55, 1.0)` remaps the mask's values and gave me a mask
    168000 sq units where I expected 25000.

The honest verdict: the picture is quiet and low-key and the drawing is sound, but everything
is too smooth. Tonn's surfaces are built out of visible, broken, varied strokes and mine are
blended into soft gradients almost everywhere. The fruit are the only passage with any brush
character. If I had another day I would stop modelling and start painting — leave the strokes
alone — especially on the table and the bowl.

I've brought the painting to a finished state.

**Title: *Quinces, Green Bottle, Low Light***

The picture is a low-key still life on a warm brown table against a dark wall. A dark green-black glass bottle stands at the back left; a wide, shallow dark bowl sits centre, holding two quinces; two more lie loose on the table in front of it. Light enters from the upper left and dies out across the picture, so the right-hand side of the table and the whole upper wall sink into shadow. The four quinces are the only light notes in the picture — olive-gold, downy, each with a small stem dimple — and everything else is kept dark so they read as the subject.

It began three days ago with a folded linen at the right, which I painted out: I could not make it read as cloth rather than a pale slab, and it was wrecking that side of the canvas. Letting the right fall away into shadow made the whole picture stronger, and I spent the rest of the work rebuilding the quinces (they had gone bald and faceted with hard yellow caps), turning the bowl from a pale lens into a dark glazed vessel, and calming the wall and table into flat, quiet fields with a proper fall of light across them.

Two things I'd flag honestly. First, my journal for this session is mostly a record of damage: I ghosted the quinces three times by blending a table mask that touched them, painted a wall glaze over the tops of the fruit because `wallm` runs behind the bowl, and lost the whole picture to one bad unifying glaze that laid pale curls over everything and had to be rebuilt. Second, the surfaces are too smooth — I modelled and blended almost everywhere, so the picture is quieter and more airbrushed than Tonn's broken, stroke-driven handling. The quinces are the only passage with real brush character in them.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers

function bbox(m, step)
  step = step or 5
  local x0,y0,x1,y1 = 1e9,1e9,-1e9,-1e9
  for y = 0, H, step do
    for x = 0, W, step do
      if m:at(x,y) > 0.5 then
        if x<x0 then x0=x end if x>x1 then x1=x end
        if y<y0 then y0=y end if y>y1 then y1=y end
      end
    end
  end
  return x0,y0,x1,y1
end

It must be the *dark* pass: rt_t at (800,480) = 0.9*clamp(320/430)=0.9*0.744=0.67 + 0.25*0 = 0.67. So the dark pass covers it. Hmm.

Fix: the table's top edge needs to be a soft transition into the wall anyway. I'll paint a dark band along the junction afterwards (ambient occlusion), which will cover the bright fringe. Also I could shrink table_m's top edge... but the mask is already painted.

So: next step, paint a soft dark band along the junction. That will both kill the fringe and create the wall/table contact shadow. 

2. The table's brushwork reads as horizontal swirls/waves — a bit repetitive, like wood grain. Acceptable for a table but the swirls are quite visible. I'd like it to be calmer.

Paint with a dark pile, coverage 2, bigb2, pressure 0.5-0.9, edge="found", clip=true. The mask is a band with a soft ramp (function mask), so strokes will be anchored where > 0.3 (within ~24 units of the junction) and clip will feather the edges. Good.

Blotchy again — the light pass with load_at produced hard-edged yellow patches.

Why do the load_at passes produce hard patches? Because with a low load the brush is nearly dry and only touches the high points of the surface (dry-brush), leaving sharp-edged marks.

That's the key: `load_at` values below ~0.4 give dry-brush deposits with hard edges.

So load_at is fundamentally unreliable here. The blend after it fixes it but flattens.

DECISION: Stop using load_at on the fruit. 

New approach for the fruit — build them as an even field plus a soft shadow:
1. Flatten with a MID pile (fq_mid3) → an even, smooth, mid-value fruit. (This alone looks like a smooth egg — not enough.)
2. Lay the shadow with an EVEN, low-contrast pass using a mask instead of load_at: use a soft-edged mask for the shadow region (an ellipse covering the lower-right of each fruit, softened a lot) with edge="loose" so it fades. Since `edge="loose"` lets the paint run past the mask and dissolve, a soft mask + loose edge gives a gradual falloff!

That's the trick: `edge="loose"` (or "soft") with a soft mask produces a gradient because the strokes thin out past the boundary. My earlier failures used edge="found" which cut sharply.

So:
- shadow mask = ellipse centred at the shadow point, radius ~1.2r, softened 20 → work(m, {pile=fq_sd2, clip=m, edge="soft"/"loose", ...}).

Wait, but edge="soft"/"lost" paints past the mask edge onto whatever is there — which for a fruit means onto the bowl/table. That's dangerous. However, if the mask is a soft gradient ellipse (values ramping to 0 at the far edge), the paint will thin out before it gets far. The overrun is "by as much as a stroke's length" though. With a filbert 12 and 20-50 unit strokes, the overrun is ~20 units. That could spill onto the table around each fruit. Hmm. But since the shadow pile is dark and the area around the fruit is a shadow anyway... risky.

Safer: clip=true AND edge="loose". Does clip=true stop the overrun? "clip=true: every bristle stops on the mask's edge" — weighted by the mask's value. My notes say edge="soft"/"lost" with clip=true still paints past the edge. Hmm, but with a SOFT mask the bristles stop earlier on average.

Honestly, the cleanest safe approach: use `work` with `hug=false` and a soft mask, coverage moderate. With hug=false, "coverage thins at the mask's edges" — that gives a fade!

So: work(soft_shadow_mask, {pile=fq_sd2, coverage=2.0, hug=false, edge="loose", clip=true, tool=fruit_b}).

That should deposit more in the middle of the mask and less toward its soft edge — a gradient!

events.text:
day 59, 06:00: Rebuilt the whole picture over nine days of painting time. What it is now: a low-key
still life on a warm brown ground — a black-green glass bottle at the back left, a wide dark glazed
bowl with two quinces sitting in it, two more quinces on the table, the light coming in from the
upper left and dying away to the right. Wall ~0.17 flat warm brown, table 0.30 (lit front left) to
0.12 (right), bottle 0.08 as a silhouette with one grey reflection down its left, bowl 0.12-0.22
with a lit rim on its front left, quinces 0.45-0.70 and they are the only light in the picture.

THE PICTURE, HONESTLY: the drawing and the value structure hold up squinting — dark band on top,
mid table across, four small bright notes in the middle — and the objects sit on the table with real
cast shadows. But it is soft everywhere: almost nothing has a found edge except the fruit, the
brushwork is mostly blended out, and the whole thing sits in one narrow band of warm brown with the
blue-black bottle as the only colour accident. It reads as a quiet, slightly over-resolved study,
not as a boldly brushed Tonn. My day-9 note said "if I had another day I would stop modelling and
start painting"; on this session I spent the day modelling again and never got there.

THE BIG TECHNICAL FINDING, and it cost me about forty chunks: there is NO reliable way to make a
soft gradient with `work` at this easel. I tried, in order —
  - `load_at` a positional function: with long strokes it lays STREAKS (each stroke starts loaded
    and runs dry, so a stroke started in the light leaves a bright ribbon), with short strokes it
    lays BLOTCHES. Low load values give dry-brush with hard edges.
  - `clip=` a soft gradient mask: bristles stop weighted by the mask value, which is patchy, not a
    gradient — visible as blobs at every scale.
  - `stipple` with `coverage` as a function: smooth ONCE (it was the best fruit I made all session),
    speckled the next four times, at any width, any cluster, any coverage.
  - `hug=false` and `edge="loose"` with a soft mask: mottled.
  - nested soft ellipses: the passes stop at the 0.3 contour, so you get a puddle with a hard rim.
THE ONE COMBINATION THAT WORKS: work() with `load_at` (blotchy as it goes down) and then `blend(m)`
inside the object mask. The blender fuses the blotches into a genuinely smooth modelled form. That
is the only recipe for a small modelled object here, and I used it on the fruit and the bowl.
And the opposite rule: for a FIELD, the only clean recipe is `hand="broad"` with a very flat
filbert (42-62), one pile, constant coverage, `edge="found", clip=true` — an even field, no streaks.

Other rules this session:
  - Paint onto SET paint or not at all. Two passes in one chunk on a wet passage came out mottled
    every time (the fruit went camo four separate times this way). One pass, then wait 18-22 h.
  - A "wash" of a transparent-ish pile over a dry passage dry-brushes and shows the underlayer;
    my cool tint on the wall turned it into torn paper. To change a whole field, flatten it with an
    OPAQUE pile at coverage 6-7 and stop.
  - A pile much darker than the one under it, laid at low coverage, does NOT knock back: it mottles
    (and it dries too transparent). Knock back means a full opaque cover at coverage 4-6.
  - After flattening a mass, the mask's soft rim survives as a pale fringe: grow the mask by 5-7
    before you paint, or flatten the ring outside the silhouette too. (I laid a ring of table colour
    around each quince twice.)
  - `outline{char="searching"}` with a big `lobe` is for a wide dry shape, never for a rim light.
  - `blend(m)` is the only smoother. It flattens, so run it last, and only inside the object mask.
  - Still true from day 1: edge="soft"/"lost" paints past the mask even with clip=true. I did it
    again with the cast shadows and wrecked the bowl and two quinces; the shadows had to be rebuilt.

THE TRAPS I FELL INTO (all mine): I chased gradients for a whole session instead of accepting even
fields; I kept re-painting areas that were already good and made them worse (the wall went from a
clean light pool to an even field and back five times); and every time I "fixed" one passage with a
new pile I broke its value and had to fix it again. The picture is better than the one I inherited —
a real bottle, a real bowl, four quinces, a proper key of light and shadows that seat them — but it
is over-smoothed, and I know exactly which pass to stop doing.

function bbox(m, step)
  step = step or 4
  local x0, y0, x1, y1, n = 1e9, 1e9, -1e9, -1e9, 0
  for y = 0, H, step do
    for x = 0, W, step do
      if m:at(x, y) > 0.5 then
        if x < x0 then x0 = x end
        if x > x1 then x1 = x end
        if y < y0 then y0 = y end
        if y > y1 then y1 = y end
        n = n + 1
      end
    end
  end
  return string.format("x %d..%d  y %d..%d  cells %d", x0, x1, y0, y1, n)
end

events.text:
day 86, ~17:00: Final session on the same picture (days 59-86). Rebuilt the whole thing again, and this time it came together.

WHAT IT IS NOW: a low-key still life. A dark green-black glass bottle at the back left, a wide dark glazed bowl with a bright lip and two quinces sitting in it, two more quinces on a warm brown table, the light coming in from the upper left and dying away to the right. Wall ~0.25 with a soft painterly grain, table ~0.30 (lit front left) to ~0.20 (right), bottle 0.06-0.12, bowl 0.08-0.14, quinces 0.40-0.70 and they are the only light in the picture. The two quinces in the bowl sit a step darker than the two on the table, so the bowl reads further back.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKED, in order of how much it mattered:
  - Flatten a field to a clean even colour FIRST: very flat filbert (40-44), hand="broad", coverage 3 at angle 0.08 then again at 1.48 with ruler=true, curve={0,0}, edge="found", clip=true, and wait(150) between. Every mess I made on the table and the wall came from NOT doing this first.
  - The bowl needed exactly ONE bright note, its lip, and one edge light on its front left. Nothing else. I tried modelling the belly three times and every version was worse than the black.
  - The fruit: dark base (coverage 4.5) -> mid over the whole fruit (2.8) -> light over a single offset ellipse crossing the fruit (2.0) -> dark crescent on the lower right (1.9) -> blend -> dark mottle at 0.9 with a filbert 7 -> deeper gold over that at 1.5 -> calyx and a couple of small highlights. That whole sequence, run without interruption, gives quinces. Running HALF of it gives potatoes.

THE TECHNICAL LESSONS THAT COST ME THE MOST (day 59's notes were right about all of these, and I broke every one of them again):
  - edge="soft" is not a soft edge, it is a licence to paint as far past the mask as a stroke is long. With 200-unit strokes and a filbert 44 it sprayed the light right across the table and left black flakes. Soft transitions are made with MANY NARROW BANDS with found edges, not with edge="soft".
  - `grow()` after subtracting objects undoes the subtraction. I flattened the wall around a glow with (mask - obj):grow(12) and the 12-unit rim came back over the bottle's whole left side and sliced the tops off the two quinces in the bowl. If you grow a mask, subtract the objects AFTERWARD.
  - A pile renders far lighter and greyer than its arithmetic value. I chased dark shadows for a whole day with browns that rendered the same as the table. The swatch test (three piles side by side on the table, then look in "value") should be the first thing I do with any new pile.
  - A low-coverage pass (< 0.8) over a big area lays WORMS, whatever the hand. On a field it is only safe if the pile is within a hair of the colour under it. On a small object it is never safe.
  - lose() on a dark shape puts black spikes round it, like grass. It is for lost edges on light paint, not for softening a shadow.
  - blend() over a fruit mask is the only thing that turns blotches into a sphere; but blend then needs re-breaking with a mottle, or the fruit comes out bald.
  - Do not alternate. Twice this session I put a veil on the two quinces in the bowl to push them back, got worms, covered the worms with gold, got flat light discs, covered those with mottle, got worms again. Each repair cost more than the original pass would have.

THE HONEST VERDICT: it is a quiet, low-key picture with sound drawing and a real key - the four quinces carry the light, the bottle and the bowl are dark anchors, and everything sits on the table with a shadow. It is still smoother than Tonn: the wall and the table are grained but even, the shadows are soft to the point of being implied rather than painted, and the mottling on the fruit is a touch close to camouflage. If I had another day the only thing I would do is break the fields harder with the flat brush and let the strokes stand.

**Quinces, Raking Light**

A low-key still life: a dark green-black glass bottle at the back left, a wide dark glazed bowl holding two quinces, and two more quinces on a warm brown table, the light coming in from the upper left and dying away into shadow at the right. The four quinces are the only light note in the picture — mottled olive-gold with dark speckling and a dry calyx at the crown — and the two in the bowl sit a step darker than the two in front so the bowl reads further back. The bowl itself is almost pure black: it is drawn by a single bright warm line along its near lip, which crosses in front of the fruit, and a thin edge light down its front-left; the bottle is held together by a green-grey turn, two broken white glints and a warm bounce off the table.

What I know is still not right, and would be the first thing I attack with another day: the wall and the table are grained but even, and Tonn's fields are built of visible standing strokes — mine are laid down and smoothed — and the fruit mottling runs a shade too close to camouflage in close-up.
